name: Skin lightening soaps

card.summary: Bar soaps sold to even out and lighten skin tone, usually through ingredients such as hydroquinone, kojic acid or (in illicit products) mercury.
card.note: Some products have been found to contain mercury; mercury and high-dose hydroquinone are banned or restricted in many countries.

quick.overview:
Skin lightening soaps are wash-off bars marketed to brighten complexion, fade dark spots and give a lighter, more even skin tone. People use them as a low-cost, easy-to-apply route toward the lighter or more uniform skin that some beauty ideals favor.

The active ingredients vary by product. Reported ones include hydroquinone, kojic acid and, in unregulated products, inorganic mercury. A 2001 study in Kenya found mercury in soaps sold around Lake Victoria and linked their wide use to possible mercury exposure.
quick.how: The soaps are used as an ordinary wash on the face or body, often daily and often alongside lightening creams. Because the product is rinsed off, contact time with skin is short, and users commonly combine it with other lightening products.
quick.risks: Mercury can cause neurological and kidney harm, and hydroquinone has been linked to ochronosis and dermatitis. Regulators in the EU and elsewhere restrict these ingredients, though enforcement varies and some banned products remain on sale. Treated skin can also be more sensitive to sun.

lead: Skin lightening soaps are cleansing bars sold with the promise of a lighter or more even skin tone. In looksmaxxing and wider beauty culture, they sit within the broader practice of skin lightening, which people pursue to reduce dark patches or to move toward a lighter complexion [3].

Products differ widely. Some use legal active ingredients such as kojic acid; others have been found to contain hydroquinone or inorganic mercury, which are restricted or banned in many jurisdictions [3]. A study published in 2001 found that mercury-containing toilet soap was available around Lake Victoria in Kenya and proposed that habitual use could contribute to mercury poisoning [1].
Published work on soaps specifically is limited to product-contamination and exposure studies rather than trials of cosmetic benefit.

chain: Lightening agent in a wash-off bar
Reduced melanin production or surface bleaching
angle.text: Users wash with the bar daily hoping to fade dark marks and lighten overall tone. Marketing describes brighter, more uniform skin; the ingredients that do this are the same restricted agents regulators discuss.

infobox: Mercury and hydroquinone restricted in many regions [3]

paras: Skin lightening soaps are bars or liquid washes presented as brightening or bleaching cleansers. Wider skin-lightening products use agents such as hydroquinone, which reduces melanin production, kojic acid, corticosteroids and others [3].

Inorganic mercury is often hidden in lightening products, and the World Health Organization has flagged it; it is linked to neurological and kidney problems [3]. The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000, and South Africa began banning mercury and high-hydroquinone formulations in the 1970s. Enforcement is described as uneven, and some banned products are still sold [3].

No clinical trials of lightening efficacy for soaps were found. Exposure research includes a 2001 study in Kenya that identified mercury-containing soaps on sale around Lake Victoria and reported that wide use might cause mercury poisoning [1]. A 2017 Ethiopian study of mercury in hair around Lake Tana concerned fish consumption and is not about soaps [2].

Reported harms of lightening agents include mercury-related neurological and kidney problems, hydroquinone-associated ochronosis and contact dermatitis, and steroid-related skin thinning when potent steroids are overused. Lightened skin can be more vulnerable to sun damage, and pregnancy exposure is a concern [3].

Lightening practices date back at least to around 200 BC, with natural ingredients like honey. Preferences have been linked by historians to class, colonialism and caste, and market use has been reported as high in several countries, for example 77 percent of Nigerian women in a 2013 figure [3].

timeline.event: South Africa begins regulating lightening products, banning mercury and high-hydroquinone formulas [3]
Researchers sample soaps around Lake Victoria, Kenya [1]
